title: The Painted Will
premise: Paloma Kavanagh, coroner of the coastal town of Bellhaven, has certified every death there for fifteen years — including the drowning of matriarch Eileen Voss. When an anonymous confession letter arrives claiming Eileen was poisoned and that the sole witness, a woman officially declared dead in 2009, is alive, Paloma reopens the case against the wishes of the powerful Voss family, who control the will leaving everything to the town. As the anniversary dinner approaches — the deadline when the will's charitable clause becomes irreversible — Paloma discovers the letter was written by her own late mentor, and that the 'dead' witness is Eileen's estranged daughter hiding under a new name. In the climax at the anniversary dinner, Paloma exposes the poisoner — the family lawyer who altered the will — and the witness comes forward, voiding the fraudulent bequest and freeing Paloma to choose love over the duty that has defined her.
about_author: Theo Joubert is a former small-town newspaper reporter from the Atlantic coast of Canada who covered coroners' inquests for a decade before turning to fiction. He lives in a converted lighthouse keeper's cottage with his wife and an ill-tempered gull he refuses to name.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She walks Bellhaven's cemetery the morning of Eileen Voss's burial, cataloguing the dead she's certified over fifteen years, establishing her meticulous, guarded character. She signs the drowning certificate without hesitation. Emotional beat: quiet pride in order — and the first hairline crack of doubt she refuses to name.

chapters.title: Postmarked the Day After
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A letter arrives claiming Eileen Voss was poisoned with digitalis and that a witness — listed as dead since 2009 — saw everything. The postmark is dated the day after the funeral. Paloma cross-checks the handwriting against old files. Emotional beat: dread curdling into obsession.

chapters.title: The Voss Table
chapters.summary: Paloma attends the funeral reception at Voss House under professional pretense. She observes the heirs: son Aldous, brittle daughter-in-law Marguerite, and lawyer Corwin Hale, executor of the will. Hale watches her watching him. Emotional beat: the sensation of being a guest at a table where everyone knows the menu but her.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years of Certificates
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, with flashback to her mentor Dr. Ambrose Fenn, who trained her and died two years ago. She reopens Eileen's file and finds Fenn's initials on an amended toxicology page. Emotional beat: loyalty to her teacher warring with the truth in her own filing cabinet.

chapters.title: A Woman Declared Dead
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She pulls the 2009 death certificate of Lena Voss, Eileen's estranged daughter — signed, she realizes with a chill, by Fenn himself. No body was ever released. Emotional beat: the ground tilting; her mentor's fingerprints are on every loose thread.

chapters.title: Aldous at the Breakwater
chapters.summary: Paloma interviews Aldous Voss on the breakwater where Eileen allegedly fell. He is grieving, defensive, and lets slip that the will leaves Voss House and land to the town — unless challenged before the anniversary dinner. Emotional beat: sympathy for a man who may be lying, and Paloma's first sense of the clock ticking.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Garden
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. In Marguerite's garden she finds foxglove — the source of digitalis — and a burned letter fragment in the fire pit. Marguerite catches her and, instead of denying, whispers: 'You think I'm the only one who wanted her gone?' Emotional beat: the case stops being about one suspect.

chapters.title: Corwin Hale's Ledger
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She discovers Hale has been quietly siphoning from the estate for years, and that the charitable clause in the will — the one expiring at the anniversary dinner — would expose his embezzlement at audit. Emotional beat: motive crystallizes; Hale is no longer just a lawyer but the man with everything to lose.

chapters.title: The Letter in Fenn's Hand
chapters.summary: Paloma compares the confession letter to Fenn's old case notes: same hand. Her dead mentor wrote it — mailed by someone after his death. She visits Fenn's sealed cottage office. Emotional beat: grief reopened; the man who taught her to file the truth may have buried it first.

chapters.title: What Ambrose Kept
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. In Fenn's locked desk she finds a second letter, unfinished, naming 'the girl at the lighthouse' as the living witness. Someone has already searched the cottage — the drawer is empty of everything else. Emotional beat: she is not the only one hunting Lena Voss, and the other hunter is ahead of her.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Niece
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She traces 'the girl at the lighthouse' to a woman named Nora Quill, a bookbinder new to town. Their first conversation is a duel of politeness, each recognizing something in the other. Emotional beat: cautious, electric connection — and Paloma's first personal stake beyond the case.

chapters.title: Dead Woman Walking
chapters.summary: Nora's POV, first time. Nora is Lena Voss: she faked her death in 2009 with Fenn's help to escape her family, and Fenn mailed the confession on his deathbed as a debt repaid. She saw Hale tamper with Eileen's medication but stayed silent to protect her new life. Emotional beat: terror and the ache of a decade spent being no one.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Paloma and Nora grow closer — long walks, small confessions — while Paloma conceals that she knows Nora's identity, and Nora conceals hers. Emotional beat: tenderness built on mutual concealment; the reader aches at what each is not saying.

chapters.title: Someone Follows
chapters.summary: Nora's POV. She realizes she's being watched — a gray sedan, a man with Hale's firm's umbrella. Her bookshop is searched; a threatening note: 'The dinner happens either way.' Emotional beat: the past closing in; Nora must decide whether to run again or stand.

chapters.title: The Exhumation Order
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She petitions to exhume Eileen Voss, forcing a confrontation with Hale, who produces a court order blocking her and hints at her 'conflicts of interest.' The town turns on her — the coroner who disturbs graves. Emotional beat: isolation; doing right costs her the town's trust.

chapters.title: Marguerite Breaks
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Cornered by Paloma, Marguerite confesses she hated Eileen and withheld the foxglove fact out of spite, but swears she never poisoned her — and reveals she saw Hale enter Eileen's room the night she died, carrying her pill organizer. Emotional beat: a bitter woman choosing truth over resentment.

chapters.title: The Pill Organizer
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She tracks the original pill organizer, discarded as medical waste, in the clinic's incinerator logs — and finds it was signed out by Hale's clerk. Hale learns she's close and makes an offer: drop it, and he'll bury her mentor's role in Lena's false death certificate. Emotional beat: temptation — he's right that the truth will burn Fenn's name too.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years of Silence
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She confronts the full record: Fenn falsified Lena's death to save her from her family, then carried the guilt until his dying day. Paloma must decide whether exposing Hale destroys the man who made her. Emotional beat: the book's thematic crux — loyalty versus truth, and what a witness owes the dead.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Dinner
chapters.summary: Nora's POV. Nora tells Paloma she will testify — then disappears. Her shop is ransacked, her passport gone. Paloma realizes Hale intends to make Lena Voss's death certificate true before morning. Emotional beat: fear at full pitch; love against duty becomes literal.

chapters.title: The Anniversary Dinner
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. At Voss House, the town raises its glasses to seal the will's clause. Paloma arrives with the exhumation findings and the tampered medication records, and stalls the toast by demanding the lights be kept on — buying time as she searches the house for Nora. Emotional beat: a lone voice against a room full of people who want the glass raised.

chapters.title: The Living Witness
chapters.summary: Climax. Paloma finds Nora bound in the estate's old boathouse and frees her as Hale arrives; Aldous, arriving to stop the toast, sees Hale's true face for the first time. Nora stands before the assembled town as Lena Voss and names Hale as Eileen's killer. Hale is arrested; the will's fraudulent clause collapses. Emotional beat: catharsis — the dead woman speaks, and the town must hear her.

chapters.title: What the Town Owes
chapters.summary: Resolution. Paloma amends Fenn's file with the whole truth — his crime and his mercy both — and lets the town judge him. Lena reclaims her name; she and Paloma walk the cemetery together, and Paloma introduces her to the graves by name, including Eileen's, now correctly marked. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace — truth filed at last, and love chosen over duty.
